title: Why the Great Books Still Matter in a Pluralistic Society
author: Ayaan Hirsi Ali
summary: Hirsi Ali argues that in a diverse, modern society, unity depends on shared cultural knowledge, and that the Great Books remain the strongest available vehicle for that shared knowledge because the questions they wrestle with — what makes a life meaningful, how to live well — belong to everyone regardless of the tradition that first posed them. She laments that even Romeo and Juliet, the most frequently taught text in American high schools, is now typically read in excerpt rather than in full, as schools prioritize demographic 'representation' or 'decolonize' curricula rather than asking whether a work is genuinely great. Drawing on Roosevelt Montas's account of his own transformation through Great Books education and E.D. Hirsch's argument that cultural literacy is 'the only sure avenue of opportunity for disadvantaged children,' she frames the Great Books not as a parochial Western inheritance but as democratizing infrastructure that gives every citizen, regardless of background, a common foundation for civic life.
points: Her core argument locates the Great Books' value in universality, not origin: questions about the good life and the human condition don't belong exclusively to the Greeks, Romans, or Englishmen who first posed them.

Even Romeo and Juliet, the most frequently taught text in American high schools, is now typically read as an excerpt rather than in full, which she cites as evidence of curricular erosion beyond just canon debates.

Roosevelt Montas's memoir Rescuing Socrates is used as proof-of-concept: an impoverished immigrant's encounter with Great Books education was personally transformative regardless of his nationality or background.
E.D. Hirsch's claim that cultural literacy is 'the only sure avenue of opportunity for disadvantaged children' reframes shared knowledge as an equity intervention rather than an elitist inheritance.

Tocqueville's observation from Democracy in America — that instruction 'powerfully contributes to the support of a democratic republic' — is used to argue shared knowledge is infrastructure for democracy itself, not just personal enrichment.
quotes: Although Romeo & Juliet remains the most frequently taught text in American high schools, students read little overall and much of what they do read is fairly recent or far too short—an excerpt rather than a full text.

But Great Books remain great, at least in part, because of their universality. Questions about what it means to live a good life and the problems of the human condition do not belong only to the Israelites, Greeks, Romans, or Englishmen who first grappled with them.

In Rescuing Socrates: How the Great Books Changed My Life and Why They Matter for a New Generation, impoverished immigrant turned Columbia professor Roosevelt Montas describes his own education in Great Books as “transformative.

As Hirsch writes, “cultural literacy constitutes the only sure avenue of opportunity for disadvantaged children, the only reliable way of combating the social determinism that now condemns them to remain in the same social and educational condition as their parents.
